topic: The Central Limit Theorem: Finding Order in Chaos
target_audience: University students or high school seniors with basic probability knowledge

sections.title: Prerequisite: Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: Imagine a large population with diverse individual traits.
Their weights follow a very strange, non-normal distribution.
Scientist Sam arrives to study these mysterious squirrels.
animations: Fade in a crowd of 50 small circles with varying shades of gray to represent the population. Label 'Population' in #FFFFFF at the top.
Animate circles moving to form a U-shaped histogram on the screen. Label 'Non-Normal Distribution' in #FFD700.
Fade in a simple stick-figure 'Sam' with a lab coat icon next to the histogram. Label 'Scientist Sam' in #87CEEB.

sections.title: The Action: The Sampling Process
lecture_lines: Sam catches a random sample of thirty squirrels.
He calculates the average weight for this group.
This average is recorded as one sample mean.
Sam repeats this process many times over.
He creates a collection of hundreds of means.
animations: Highlight 30 random circles from the population in #00FF00. Label 'Sample (n=30)'.
Move the 30 circles to a 'calculator' [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/calculator.svg] box that outputs a single number 'Sample Mean'.
The number 'Sample Mean' transforms into a small yellow square (sticky note) and moves to the bottom.
Rapidly repeat the sampling process, with 100 sticky notes accumulating at the bottom of the screen.
The sticky notes begin to stack vertically on a horizontal line to form a rough histogram.

sections.title: The Magic: The Distribution of Sample Means
lecture_lines: Now we plot all those sample means together.
Watch the shape of the new distribution emerge.
Despite the messy population, a bell curve forms.
This is the Central Limit Theorem in action.
Randomness converges into a predictable normal shape.
animations: The sticky note stacks from Section 2 settle into a clear histogram. Label 'Distribution of Sample Means' in #FF4500.
Display the original U-shaped population distribution as a ghosted outline in #555555 for comparison.
Animate the histogram bars shifting and growing as sample size 'n' increases from 2 to 30.
Morph the histogram bars into a smooth, white (#FFFFFF) Bell Curve.
Highlight the center of the Bell Curve and label 'Normal Distribution' in #00FA9A.

sections.title: The Mathematical Mechanics
lecture_lines: For the theorem to work, sample size matters.
The distribution's center marks the true population mean.
We calculate the spread using the standard error.
Increasing the sample size makes our estimate narrower.
Larger samples lead to much higher precision.
animations: Display the text 'n ≥ 30' in large, bold #FF6347 font in the corner.
Show a vertical dashed line through the center of the Bell Curve, labeled 'μ' in #ADD8E6.
Display the formula 'σ / √n' in #F0E68C near the tail of the curve. Label 'Standard Error'.
Scale the Bell Curve horizontally (making it thinner) while increasing its height to show the effect of increasing 'n'.
Flash the central area of the narrowest curve in #FFFFFF to emphasize high precision.

sections.title: Application: Why It Matters
lecture_lines: We can predict outcomes even without knowing everything.
This makes modern quality control and polling possible.
The Central Limit Theorem finds order within chaos.
animations: Show a silhouette of a complex, unknown shape. Replace it with a predictable Bell Curve. Label 'Predictability' in #FFFFFF.
Fade in a sequence of cereal box icons on a line. Label 'Quality Control' in #DA70D6 above them.
Display 'CLT: Order from Chaos' in the center of the screen in #FFFFFF and scale it up.
